sections.heading: Ground the problem list in product experience
sections.content: In the empathize phase, put yourself in customers’ shoes and build a visual understanding of their problems. Use the product yourself and pay attention to what works or does not; Ebi says product exposure and curiosity help develop product sense. She also describes research as part of understanding foundational problems, while cautioning against defaulting to research for every question. The PM’s role is to bring clarity and context to the problems being solved, and to curate them together.

sections.heading: Maintain a living, shared inventory
sections.content: Ebi has PMs maintain a living document called “10 things you should know”: ten known product problems, revised every quarter. The problems can be qualitative, quantitative, or technical debt. This keeps the set of known problems visible and current rather than treating it as a one-time exercise.

sections.heading: Bring in other perspectives, then distill
sections.content: For strategy work—especially for platform PMs with many stakeholders—Ebi may ask teams such as marketing, operations, support, research, and content strategy to submit and stack-rank their own ten problems using the same template. She then combines those perspectives and “sandpapers” them down to the core problems and final ten. One example was learning that the average reading age of an American is 11, which prompted reconsideration of text-heavy experiences.

sections.heading: Keep the understanding circulating
sections.content: A synthesis of Ebi’s recommendations is to share the problem understanding repeatedly, invite questions, and record what the group concluded. When presenting vision work, she presented it to teams more than once because understanding took time and people needed to stress-test it; she also wrote up workshop insights, strategy, and major priorities. This can help keep the shared context alive as the team moves from problems toward vision.

answer.summary: Atawodi recommends grounding PMs in the customer’s problems, then keeping a shared, regularly updated problem list and refining it with input from stakeholders. Use written synthesis and discussion to make the core problems clear across the team.

sections.heading: Build an informed view of the problems
sections.content: In the “empathize” part of developing a vision, put yourself in the customer’s shoes: use the product yourself, observe what works or frustrates you, and use research to understand users’ problems and needs. Atawodi also encourages PMs to develop product sense by paying attention to products they use and articulating what they value.

sections.heading: Maintain a living, shared problem list
sections.content: Have each PM keep a living “top 10 things you should know” document: ten known product problems, which may be qualitative, quantitative, or technical debt. Revise it every quarter so the problem set stays current. Atawodi says the problems should be known across the organization, not held only in a PM’s head.

sections.heading: Bring in other perspectives and refine
sections.content: For strategy work, ask stakeholders—such as marketing, communications, support, research, and content strategy—to submit their own ten problems using the same template and rank them. Then combine those perspectives and “sandpaper” them down to the core problems and final list. For example, a stakeholder’s point about the average American reading age being 11 prompted reconsideration of text-heavy product content.

sections.heading: Create clarity through synthesis and communication
sections.content: The PM’s role is to bring clarity and context to the problems being solved, rather than simply relay what engineering or design says. Atawodi describes a narrative–insights–strategy–big rocks framework and says writing helps create clarity; she has teams produce two-page documents. Sharing workshop outputs and revisiting them with the team gives people a chance to ask questions and stress-test their understanding.
